notes: Sprinkler timer guide series (owner GO 2026-09-05; scope in docs/irrigation-controller-guide-scope.md). Hub-only informational posts that teach a lawn customer to run the irrigation controller on their own wall, one brand per post. GLOBAL RULES, all briefs: (1) informational lane only — no near-me or transactional phrasing anywhere; (2) MANUAL-FIRST: the primary how-to is running the controller BY HAND, following the customer's weekly Waves watering plan for that week. THE PLAN DOES NOT ALWAYS CARRY PER-ZONE MINUTES: where the head type is missing or mixed it gives an events-only "full cycle" instruction instead, so every routine needs a branch that follows the plan's own full-cycle wording rather than telling the reader to enter minutes that were never supplied. THE PLAN IS AUTHORITATIVE FOR CADENCE AND THE GUIDE NEVER HARDCODES ONE: the plan decides how many runs that week (it can be more than one on a two-day permission), and whether to skip entirely (the plan does NOT choose or name the weekday — it says only "your permitted watering day", so the assigned day or days come from the county or address lookup), and — when it asks the reader to check the rain — whether to skip an INDIVIDUAL run. So write "follow this week's plan" and "each run it asks for", never "once a week", and cover all FOUR cases the plan can present: run; check the rain before each run and skip just that one; a hold week, which is usually CONDITIONAL — the plan itself says to run a fallback cycle if the grass shows wilt cues, or if the reader did not run the previous week — so never flatten a hold into "do nothing"; and a week where watering is not permitted at all, which is the only unconditional no-watering case. Whatever the plan says that week is what the reader does: quote its condition, never replace it — OFF is the resting position between runs ONLY where every zone is manual — OFF disables all zones, so in a mixed yard whose beds or drip still run automatically the controller stays in its normal run position and the grass zones are separated out instead; wherever OFF is recommended, this qualification must appear with it; a programmed schedule is the optional section at the END of the post; (3) every controller mechanic (dial positions, button names, manual-run steps, rain delay, sensor bypass) must match the cited manufacturer manual — if the manual does not support a step, OMIT it; never invent a button. Where a manufacturer blocks automated requests and no manual can be fetched (Hunter), the owner-reviewed Waves brand guide named in that brief's sources is the authority instead, and no control it does not describe may be introduced; (4) the weekly plan NEVER names weekday(s) — it carries the number of runs and the minutes, and speaks only of 'your permitted watering day' — so a schedule section must send the reader to their county or address lookup for the assigned weekday(s) and use the plan only for how many runs and how long; NEVER state a number of allowed watering days per week, an assigned weekday, or allowed hours — watering-day rules come from the customer's county and the current water-shortage order and change; say 'your assigned day and your county's allowed hours' and point to the county; (5) a hand run counts the same as a scheduled one for those rules — say so; (6) Waves does NOT repair irrigation: if a zone will not run, a head is broken, or the box faults, the reader is referred to an irrigation contractor — never imply Waves services, installs, or repairs sprinklers; (7) never describe any product or application as 'safe'; never state prices or dollar amounts — for controller pricing say 'check current pricing'; (8) no manufacturer imagery or scraped photos: hero and body images are generated or Waves-owned, and no manual text is reproduced — link the official manual instead; (9) the weekly Waves watering plan may be mentioned only as 'the weekly watering plan Waves lawn customers receive' — never promise it names the day, never state how many runs it will ask for, and never imply it always asks for the same number; (10) internal links: the lawn treatment prep page and the overwatering-vs-underwatering post at minimum. (11) every post links one lawn care city service page (/lawn-care-{city}-fl/) in the body — the quality gate's hub-link hard check requires it.

briefs.thesis: Rain Bird's dial controllers (ESP-TM2, ESP-Me/Me3) are among the timers we most often find on Southwest Florida homes and straightforward to run by hand once you know the dial — which is all most homeowners need (make no cross-brand ranking; no source here compares brands): a hand run for each run this week's plan asks for, with that week's minutes (the plan may ask for more than one, for none, or for a rain check before each), the dial back on OFF between runs where every zone is manual, and the programmed schedule left for the few who want it. Frame prevalence explicitly as our own field experience; state no market share, ranking or figure, and attribute it to no source.
outline: Quick answer: which Rain Bird you have (where the model name is printed) and the weekly move — do exactly what THIS week's plan asks: a hand run with this week's minutes for EACH run it calls for (it may call for more than one), on a hold week, exactly what the plan says — those weeks usually carry a condition (run a fallback cycle if the grass wilts, or if you missed last week's run), so read it rather than assuming "do nothing", and when it asks you to check the rain, that check before each individual run; then back to OFF between runs where every zone is manual (keep the normal run position if beds or drip have their own schedules)

A short history of Rain Bird: founded 1933 in Glendora, California, around Orton Englehart's horizontal-action impact sprinkler; still family-owned; headquartered in Azusa — verified against rainbird.com/about, dates omitted if the page does not state them

The models you will actually find on a Southwest Florida wall: ESP-TM2 (the builder-grade dial box we routinely find on newer homes — field experience only, no "most" and no market-share claim), ESP-Me and ESP-Me3 (expandable, up to 22 zones, LNK2 Wi-Fi option on the Me3), ESP-RZXe (button faceplate, no dial), SST (simple push-button unit) — one paragraph each, what the faceplate looks like, who it suits

Honest review — pros (as our own hands-on opinion, explicitly labelled as such, never as a sourced ranking): the dial programming is straightforward; manual watering is one dial position; Seasonal Adjust is one knob; parts and manuals are everywhere; cons: multiple start-time slots per program hide an inherited builder schedule, and how many slots and programs a model has differs between them — take the count from that model's own manual rather than quoting one number for the range; the OFF position is the only sure resting state; the Wi-Fi module costs extra; the SST has no per-zone flexibility beyond its buttons. Include a ComparisonTable of the four models (dial or buttons, max zones, manual-run control, Wi-Fi option, best for) with NO prices, and an HonestRejection: who should not bother upgrading or programming a schedule at all

How to run it by hand, per model (HowTo, visible numbered steps): ESP-TM2 — MANUAL STATION is a ONE-ZONE operation, so describe it as such; BEFORE any stored-program run, update RUN TIMES for every grass zone to the minutes in THIS week's plan — the plan recalculates them from current demand and carryover, so a stored number goes stale — then for the whole lawn use the stored-program manual start the linked manual gives (dial to AUTO RUN, select the program, hold the start control until it begins), exactly as the published Waves Rain Bird guide already describes it; ESP-Me3 — dial to Manual Watering, set minutes, press Hold to Start until STARTED, turn the dial to AUTO. ESP-Me: only the Me3 manual is cited here, so do NOT apply the Me3 sequence to the Me — describe the faceplate and point the reader to the Rain Bird support center for that model, unless its own manual is added to sources and the steps verified against it; RZXe and SST — no manual for either model is cited in this brief, so give NO button sequence for them: describe what the faceplate looks like and send the reader to the Rain Bird support center for that model's own instructions. Mixed yards (grass plus bed or drip zones): store per-zone minutes, refresh them from each week's plan, and start the grass program by hand, or run grass zones one at a time. After a run, return the dial to OFF the same day ONLY when every zone is manual — if beds or drip still run on their own schedules, leave the dial in its normal run position instead, or OFF disables their watering indefinitely

Why OFF is the resting position, and the one-time check: with the dial on OFF nothing waters (Rain Bird's own manual says so); before the first hand run, step through EVERY start-time slot in EVERY program the model has — the count differs by model, so take it from that model's manual rather than assuming three programs and four slots — and set to OFF only the slots belonging to grass-only programs, so a builder's leftover lawn schedule cannot fire while the dial sits in a run position. In a mixed yard, LEAVE the start times that drive bed or drip programs alone and remove the grass zones from those programs instead; clearing their starts is the same mistake as leaving the dial on OFF

Watering rules: a hand run counts the same as a scheduled one — run it only on your assigned day and inside your county's allowed hours; those come from the county and the current water-shortage order and change, so check the county page; Waves lawn customers get a weekly watering plan with the minutes per zone and what to do that week — which may be one run or more than one, a rain check before each run, or a hold that usually still carries a condition

Want it to run itself? The optional schedule (dial models): DATE/TIME with AM/PM checked twice, ONE program verified to hold grass zones only - use an unused program if program A already drives beds or drip, and never repoint an existing non-turf program - one start time chosen so the WHOLE cycle — the sum of every enabled zone's run time — both begins and finishes inside the allowed hours, with the other slots OFF, RUN TIMES per zone, RUN DAYS = the assigned day or days for your address, which you take from your county's watering-restriction lookup (the weekly plan never names weekdays — it gives you how many runs and how many minutes), setting every assigned day the plan's run count needs, dial back to AUTO RUN; A schedule does NOT end the weekly job: it repeats a fixed cadence and fixed minutes, so tell the reader that when a later weekly plan changes the minutes they must update the stored run times, and when the plan says to SKIP they must suppress that week's run (rain delay, or clearing the grass program's start for that week) rather than letting a stale schedule water through a rain-covered week. If the reader suppresses a scheduled run by clearing the grass program's start time, they must take care when the plan asks for more than one run: a single start time is shared by every selected run day, so clearing it to skip ONE event also cancels the later ones the plan may still want (under a rain-check plan the second run happens unless another half inch falls after the first permitted day). Use a suppression scoped to that single event where the model offers one; otherwise write the original start down and restore it BEFORE the next assigned day, not the next week — a cleared start stays cleared, so an unrestored one disables the turf schedule for good. Prefer a mechanism that expires on its own where the model offers one. rain delay (ONLY where every automatic program may pause together — a controller-wide delay also stops bed and drip programs, so in a mixed yard suppress the grass program alone instead) = dial on AUTO RUN, hold the + button, set days remaining (up to 14); leave SEASONAL ADJUST at 100% because a percentage set once scales every later run-time entry. Rain-sensor handling differs between these models — give the control path each model's own linked manual describes, under that model's heading, and do not present one sensor control as if every model had it; note that a hand-started run may ignore the sensor where the manual says so The plan can also change HOW MANY runs it asks for from one week to the next, so the scheduled run days must be refreshed too — not just the minutes — or the controller keeps last week's cadence.

When the sprinklers will not run: Waves does not repair irrigation — a zone that will not come on, a broken head, or a box fault goes to an irrigation contractor; Waves still tells you what to water and when

FAQ (4–6 questions): where is the model name; does OFF erase my programs (no); why did my sprinklers come on at noon (AM/PM); can I run one zone only; what does Seasonal Adjust do; do I need the Wi-Fi module

The optional schedule is maintained weekly, exactly like the manual routine: refresh the stored run times when the plan changes the minutes, refresh the scheduled RUN DAYS / Water Days when the plan changes how many runs it asks for, and suppress a run the plan does not want. Write every routine as "do what this week's plan says, for each run it asks for". Never say "once a week" and never treat skip as an all-or-nothing week.

Any controller-wide pause (rain delay, SYSTEM OFF, OFF) stops EVERY zone. Wherever one is offered, say so and give mixed-yard readers a grass-program-only alternative — this is the same failure mode as the OFF advice, in a different control.

Stored minutes go stale: the weekly plan recalculates minutes from current demand and carryover, so every stored-program run must be preceded by updating RUN TIMES for the grass zones from that week's plan. Never write "store the minutes once".

A hold ("skip") week is usually CONDITIONAL: the plan tells the reader to run a fallback cycle if the grass shows wilt cues, or if they did not run the previous week. Never write "skip means do nothing" as a blanket rule — say to follow the plan's own wording for that week, and reserve unconditional no-watering for a week where irrigation is not permitted at all.

The weekly plan does not name weekdays and cannot: it says "your permitted watering day". Anywhere the reader must choose RUN DAYS / Water Days, send them to their county or address lookup for the assigned day(s), and use the plan only for how many runs and how many minutes.

With a grass-only program A: when this week's plan says to water, set THIS week's minutes under Run Times, dial to RUN, hold the right arrow about two seconds to start it, then back to SYSTEM OFF when it finishes (only if every zone is manual); on a hold week, do exactly what the plan says — those weeks usually carry a condition (run a fallback cycle if the grass wilts, or if you missed last week's run) rather than meaning "do nothing". Hydrawise (HC / Pro-HC / HPC) has no dial: send those readers straight to the app-and-touchscreen section instead of any dial sequence

Hydrawise owners: run grass zones from the app or touchscreen for the plan’s minutes, schedule beds and drip SEPARATELY according to their own irrigation guidance — do not tell readers those zones need shorter runs than turf; emitter output and plant demand set those durations, and the weekly plan’s minutes are turf-only — and remove grass zones from automatic programs rather than deleting programs other zones still need
